strengths: Timely and practically relevant topic: systematic benchmarking of compressed large reasoning models (quantization, distillation, pruning) is underexplored, and the paper fills a genuine gap.

Reasonably broad coverage: three major compression paradigms, multiple bit-widths (2.51/1.73/1.58-bit), seven sparsity levels, and two student model families, evaluated across four diverse reasoning benchmarks of varying difficulty.

The attempt to disentangle knowledge memorization from reasoning capability (via closed-book MuSiQue vs. reasoning-only benchmarks) is an interesting framing, and the collapse-point analysis across sparsity levels and task difficulty is informative.

The test-time compute (output length vs. accuracy) analysis and the qualitative case study of collapse behavior (repetitive generation) add behavioral insights beyond raw scores, and the setup details (models, inference frameworks, hyperparameters, benchmark sources) are documented clearly enough to aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is weak: single-pass evaluation at temperature 0.6 on very small test sets (AIME 2024 has only 30 questions; MuSiQue is sampled down to 100), with no multiple runs, no variance/standard errors, and no significance testing. Several headline conclusions (e.g., 2.51-bit surpassing full R1, or differences of a few accuracy points) are within plausible sampling noise.

The central claim that 'parameter count has a much greater impact on knowledge than reasoning' is confounded: it rests essentially on comparing R1-Distill-Qwen (32B) vs. R1-Distill-Llama (70B), but these differ in base model family, pretraining data, and distillation data—not just parameter count. Attributing the MuSiQue gap to parameter size alone is not supported; a controlled comparison (e.g., students of different sizes from the same family) is missing.

Coverage of compression methods is narrow despite claims of comprehensiveness: quantization is only Unsloth dynamic quantization (no GPTQ/AWQ/comparison), and pruning is only SparseGPT applied to distilled dense models rather than the MoE R1 itself, which limits the generality of the recommendations.

The test-time compute analysis is purely correlational (shorter outputs score better) and largely confirms prior findings (cited Zhang et al., 2024b); treating words as tokens and threshold-based bucketing further weaken the analysis. No causal intervention or verbosity-reduction experiment is attempted.

Baseline/calibration issues: the anomaly that 2.51-bit R1 beats uncompressed R1 via the API is attributed speculatively to 'security mechanisms' without investigation; including a local FP16/BF16 R1 baseline (or reporting API failure rates and retry protocol) would strengthen the comparison.

Novelty of insights is moderate: the findings (quantization preserves reasoning better than pruning/distillation; high sparsity causes collapse/repetition; verbosity correlates with errors) are plausible and partially known from the LLM compression literature; the paper is primarily an empirical report rather than a methodological contribution.
Some scope limitations are under-justified: only one LRM (DeepSeek-R1) is studied, so conclusions about 'LRMs' in general may not generalize to other reasoning models.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant topic: systematic evaluation of quantization, distillation, and pruning on large reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 family) is underexplored, and the paper covers all three major compression paradigms in one framework.

Reasonable benchmark diversity spanning mathematical (AIME 2024), logical (FOLIO), temporal (BIG-Bench Hard Temporal Sequences), and multihop/knowledge-intensive (MuSiQue) reasoning, with a useful closed-book setup to probe parametric knowledge.
The collapse-point analysis across sparsity levels (10%–80%) and the qualitative case study of repetitive-generation collapse are informative and concrete.

The test-time compute (output length vs. accuracy) analysis, while correlational, connects to a relevant ongoing discussion about verbosity in reasoning chains and could inform efficient reasoning research.
weaknesses: Statistically weak evaluation: a single pass per benchmark with no variance reported. Several key claims rest on very small effective sample sizes (e.g., AIME 2024 has only 30 questions, so a 3.3% difference is a single question; MuSiQue is subsampled to 100). Differences like '2.51-bit R1 surpasses the original R1' or 'shorter outputs are better' could easily be noise; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple sampling passes are provided.

The headline claim that 'parameter count has a much greater impact on knowledge memorization than on reasoning capability' is drawn almost entirely from a single confounded comparison (Qwen-32B vs. LLaMA-70B on MuSiQue). Base-model pretraining data and quality differ between Qwen and LLaMA, so size is not isolated; the causal conclusion is over-claimed relative to the evidence.

The test-time compute finding is largely a selection artifact: conditioning on per-question output length and observing that short outputs are more accurate conflates difficulty with verbosity—models naturally spend more tokens on harder questions (or on failures requiring backtracking). The paper acknowledges correlation but still draws prescriptive conclusions ('need to reduce verbosity') without any intervention (e.g., length-penalized decoding, forced-conciseness experiments) to support causality.

The 'benchmark' lacks methodological novelty or controlled comparison: it evaluates off-the-shelf artifacts (Unsloth GGUF quantizations, official R1 distills) rather than applying compression methods under matched settings. Cross-method comparisons are confounded by different base/student models and inference stacks (llama.cpp vs. vLLM vs. DeepSeek API), and the authors' own explanation for R1 underperforming its 2.51-bit quantization (API safety filtering with iterative re-prompting) further undermines the reliability of the reference scores.

Limited scope and generality: only one model family (DeepSeek-R1 lineage) and one pruning algorithm (SparseGPT) are studied; no baselines from the existing LRM compression literature are compared against, so the empirical landscape is narrow.

Analysis is mostly descriptive: findings such as collapse-point-vs.-difficulty correlation are stated from eyeballing small tables without any statistical treatment, and several 'recommendations' (e.g., prefer quantization when knowledge matters) are generic and derivable from prior LLM compression work.

Reproducibility and rigor gaps: no released code or prompts, unclear answer-extraction/grading procedures for EM/F1 on free-form outputs, and the random MuSiQue subsample is not specified. Inconsistent, informal writing ('due to it large parameter count', 'SpraseGPT', 'Works has been done') further suggests insufficient polish.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: systematically benchmarking quantization, distillation, and pruning of large reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 family) on diverse reasoning tasks (math, logic, temporal, multihop) fills a genuine gap, since most compression work evaluates only perplexity or simple tasks.

The paper goes beyond raw scores and studies model behavior: collapse points across sparsity levels, a knowledge-vs-reasoning decomposition via closed-book MuSiQue, and a test-time compute (output length) analysis. The finding that parameter count disproportionately affects knowledge memorization compared to reasoning capability is an actionable insight for practitioners choosing compression methods.

Reasonable breadth of compression configurations: three dynamic quantization levels (2.51/1.73/1.58-bit), two distilled students (LLaMA-70B, Qwen-32B), and seven sparsity levels via SparseGPT, with collapse-point analysis correlating sparsity tolerance with benchmark difficulty.
Qualitative case study of collapse behavior (repetitive generation at high sparsity) adds useful descriptive value, and the paper is generally clear and well organized with RQs explicitly stated.
Evaluation setup largely follows the official DeepSeek-R1 inference settings (max length 32768, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95), and released model checkpoints/links support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is weak. AIME 2024 has only 30 questions and MuSiQue only 100 sampled questions, with a single pass per model. With temperature 0.6 sampling, differences of a few points (e.g., 76.7 vs 73.3 on AIME, or EM differences of 1-2 points) are well within noise, yet the paper draws method-level conclusions (e.g., '2.51-bit has the best overall performance') without confidence intervals, multiple passes (pass@k or majority voting), or significance tests.

The central confound in the R1 comparison is acknowledged but unresolved: the original R1 via API underperforms the 2.51-bit quantized model, attributed to 'security mechanisms' and iterative prompting to avoid empty responses. This makes the R1 baseline unreliable and undermines cross-method comparisons (quantization vs distillation vs pruning), since the R1 numbers appear depressed.

Only one LRM family (DeepSeek-R1) is studied, and the 'shorter outputs achieve better performance' analysis is post-hoc and correlational: selecting the shortest/longest 30% of responses per benchmark mixes question difficulty with verbosity (harder questions elicit longer backtracking). The paper does not control for question-level difficulty, so the causal claim that verbosity hurts reasoning is not established; the finding also largely echoes prior work (e.g., Zhang et al., 2024b) they cite.

The headline claim that 'parameter count has a much greater impact on knowledge memorization than reasoning capability' rests mainly on the MuSiQue comparison of two distilled models (Qwen-32B vs LLaMA-70B), which differ in base model family and training data as well as size. This is a thin basis for such a general conclusion; a knowledge-only task (e.g., closed-book QA) vs reasoning-only decomposition with more model pairs would be needed.

Limited novelty in methodological contribution: the paper benchmarks existing artifacts (Unsloth quantized checkpoints, official DeepSeek distills, off-the-shelf SparseGPT) rather than proposing new techniques, and no additional compression methods (e.g., AWQ, GPTQ, Wanda, structured pruning) are compared, limiting the comprehensiveness the paper claims.

Inference is run on heterogeneous stacks (llama.cpp for quantized models, vLLM for distilled/pruned, DeepSeek API for full R1) while token counting uses a word-based proxy instead of a tokenizer, both of which introduce inconsistencies the paper itself acknowledges but does not quantify.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('it large parameter count', 'SpraseGPT', 'top match challenges'), citation formatting problems (e.g., 'Daniel Han & team' as author), and key experimental details (prompts used, answer extraction rules) deferred or underspecified, which hurts reproducibility.

strengths: Comprehensive and timely empirical benchmarking: the paper covers all three major compression paradigms (quantization, distillation, pruning) across 4 model families and many methods (Unsloth dynamic quantization, AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3, SparseGPT), evaluated on four reasoning benchmarks with varying difficulty — a useful and thorough resource for practitioners.

Mechanistic interpretability is a novel lens for analyzing compression effects on LRMs; adapting difference-of-means steering vectors and attribution patching to quantify per-module weight importance in compressed LRMs is a sensible and interesting methodological choice.

The paper does not stop at observation: it validates its interpretability claims with intervention experiments — selectively quantizing the top-ranked module (32_up) causes a 16.3% average accuracy drop, and selectively protecting ~2% of weights recovers +6.57% average accuracy over 3-bit AWQ, providing causal support for the main findings.

Interesting and actionable findings, e.g., weight count affects knowledge memorization more than reasoning, collapse points correlate with benchmark difficulty, and final-layer MLP up_proj importance — complementing prior work (Shao & Wu, 2025) that implicates o_proj.
Useful supplementary analyses including test-time compute vs. correctness, model collapse case studies, and sparsity sweep collapse points.
weaknesses: Limited generality of the mechanistic analysis: the weight-importance interpretation is only performed on two small models (R1-Distill-Llama-8B and R1-Distill-Qwen-7B). It is unclear whether the conclusions (final-layer up_proj importance, gate_proj over-compression) generalize to 32B/70B models or to the full R1, yet the paper's claims are framed generally.

Statistical fragility of the evaluation: AIME 2024 has only 30 questions and MuSiQue is a 100-question subsample, so per-benchmark scores have very high variance (3.3% granularity on AIME), and only three runs are used. Several headline numbers (e.g., +6.57%) could fall within noise margins; no significance testing is provided.

The validation of the protection mechanism (Table 4) is narrow: it is tested on a single model (R1-Distill-Llama-8B), a single quantizer (AWQ), and only on the full-precision final-layer MLP. There is no comparison against protecting other equally-sized modules or other mixed-precision baselines, so 'greatly surpassing the state-of-the-art' is an over-claim.

The 'importance shift' analysis sets all increases in relative importance to zero by an ad hoc convention (Section 2.3); the resulting heatmaps and conclusions could be sensitive to this choice, and no ablation or alternative normalization is discussed.

Attribution patching is a first-order linear approximation, and the behavioral token labels (backtracking, uncertainty estimation, example testing, adding knowledge) are obtained by prompting GPT-4o, introducing label noise; neither limitation is analyzed.
The 'knowledge vs. reasoning' finding rests almost entirely on a single closed-book MuSiQue proxy; other knowledge-intensive evaluations would strengthen this claim.

Some inconsistencies weaken confidence: 1_up does not follow the predicted rank-accuracy correlation, and the interpretation pipeline is described only sparsely (e.g., the footnote 'Our interpretation code is a' is an incomplete sentence), hurting reproducibility and polish.

Novelty is moderate: the core techniques (difference of means, attribution patching, behavioral taxonomy) are adopted from Venhoff et al. (2025), Arditi et al. (2024), and Syed et al. (2023); the contribution is primarily their application to compressed LRMs plus empirical benchmarking.

strengths: Timely and relevant question: systematically studying how quantization, distillation, and pruning affect large reasoning models is useful for the efficiency community.

Breadth of benchmarking: Table 1 covers many compression configurations (dynamic quantization, AWQ/GPTQ/GPTAQ/ANY4/ANY3, SparseGPT) across four model scales and four reasoning benchmarks, plus sparsity sweep analysis (Table 2).

The paper attempts to close the loop between interpretability findings and actionable compression improvements (validation via selective quantization in Table 3 and a mixed-precision protection experiment in Table 4).
Appendices provide useful auxiliary analyses (test-time compute, collapse case studies) that go beyond the core claims.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: difference-of-means steering vectors and attribution patching are directly adapted from Arditi et al. (2024), Syed et al. (2023), and Venhoff et al. (2025). The core contribution is an empirical application of existing interpretability tools, and the paper positions itself mainly against one recent workshop paper.

Several headline findings are expected or already known: 4-bit quantization preserves reasoning while 3-bit degrades, pruning destroys knowledge retention, and compression collapse correlates with benchmark difficulty have been reported in prior empirical studies (e.g., Liu et al., 2025), which weakens the claimed contribution.

Attribution patching is a first-order (linear) approximation of causal importance, yet the paper draws strong causal conclusions ('most important weights'). The validation is thin: only a handful of candidate components are selectively quantized (Table 3), on a single 8B model, with no statistical significance testing given the very small test sets (AIME has only 30 problems; MuSiQue is 100 sampled questions; even averaged over 3 runs, differences of a few points are within noise).

The interpretability analysis is performed only on small models (Llama-8B, Qwen-7B) while benchmarking spans up to 70B/671B; generalization of the final-layer up_proj finding across scales is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The central practical claim ('protecting just 2% of weights raises accuracy by 6.57%, greatly surpassing the state-of-the-art') is overclaimed: it is validated on exactly one model (R1-Distill-Llama-8B), one quantizer (AWQ), and a single hand-crafted mixed-precision configuration; no comparison against existing mixed-precision or importance-aware quantization baselines (e.g., AWQ's own salience metrics, SparseGPT-style importance scores, OmniQuant).

The 'importance shift' analysis conflates compression effects with distribution shifts and normalization artifacts; the choice to zero out increases in relative importance (Section 2.3) is a design decision that could systematically shape the reported heatmaps, with limited sensitivity analysis.
Contradiction with prior work (Shao & Wu, 2025, claiming o_proj is most important) is noted but not resolved or explained beyond a one-sentence remark.

Reproducibility concerns: the interpretation code footnote is incomplete ('Our interpretation code is a'), and no code release is committed; prompts used for GPT-4o behavior labeling are not shown, though this labeling is a critical pipeline component.
Presentation quality is below venue standard: typos ('interpretaion', 'imrpving', 'top match challenges'), an incomplete footnote, and takeaways that sometimes restate the obvious reduce polish.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant topic: a systematic benchmark of quantization (Unsloth dynamic, AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3), distillation (R1-distilled Llama/Qwen), and pruning (SparseGPT) applied to DeepSeek-R1 variants, which existing literature has not comprehensively covered for LRMs.

Novel angle connecting mechanistic interpretability (difference-of-means steering vectors + attribution patching) to the compression problem of locating critical weights, going beyond prior layer-level analyses (e.g., Venhoff et al.) to per-module weight importance.

Findings are empirically validated rather than merely observed: selective 3-bit quantization of the final-layer up_proj (Table 3) confirms the importance ranking, and a simple mixed-precision protection of final-layer MLP modules yields a consistent 6.57% average gain (Table 4), demonstrating actionable value.

Broad coverage of sparsity levels and bit-widths (Tables 1-2), yielding useful practical guidance such as collapse points correlating with benchmark difficulty and quantization being preferable for knowledge-intensive tasks.

Useful supplementary analyses on test-time compute (shorter responses correlate with correctness) and model collapse behavior with qualitative case studies, adding practical insight for LRM deployment.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core techniques (difference of means, attribution patching) are adapted from prior work; the contribution is primarily an empirical study and analysis, which may limit impact.

Very small evaluation sets undermine statistical reliability: AIME 2024 has only 30 problems, and only 100 of 1000 MuSiQue questions are sampled; with three passes, many reported differences (e.g., the 6.57% protection gain, GPTAQ vs. GPTQ comparisons) likely fall within noise, yet no significance testing or confidence intervals are provided.

Interpretation analysis is confined to the smallest models (Llama-8B and Qwen-7B distilled variants); the claim that findings generalize is based on only two model families, and the mechanistic conclusions may not transfer to larger LRMs.

The headline claim of 'greatly surpassing the state-of-the-art' is overstated: the mixed-precision protection result is demonstrated only on R1-Distill-Llama-8B with 3-bit AWQ (a single model, single method, small benchmarks), and the gain is modest relative to full-precision baselines.

Some takeaways are relatively expected or weakly supported as causal claims: e.g., 'pruning/distillation hurts knowledge more than reasoning' is inferred from aggregate benchmark comparisons and cross-family confounds (Qwen vs. Llama differ in more than parameter count), and importance-shift analysis compares different backbone architectures (Llama-8B vs. Qwen2.5-Math-7B), complicating attribution of effects to distillation alone.
The four 'reasoning behaviors' are token-labeled by prompting GPT-4o, introducing label noise that is not quantified or validated, which propagates into the steering vectors and importance scores.

Reproducibility concerns: the footnote stating the interpretation code is available appears truncated/incomplete ('Our interpretation code is a'), and some implementation details (calibration data for quantization, prompt formats) are deferred without full specification.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant question: how quantization, distillation, and pruning affect the reasoning capabilities of large reasoning models (LRMs), an area where existing work is indeed sparse

Comprehensive benchmarking across three compression paradigms, multiple methods (AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3, SparseGPT, AlphaPruning, dynamic quantization) and four model scales, with three evaluation runs to mitigate variability

Novel adaptation of mechanistic interpretability techniques (difference of means + attribution patching) to compute fine-grained, module-level weight importance for reasoning behaviors, going beyond layer-wise analysis

Findings are not just observational: they are validated empirically (selective 3-bit quantization of the final-layer up projection causes a 16.3% drop; protecting ~2% of weights yields a 6.57% average gain over 3-bit AWQ), and the authors provide cross-checks against AWQ scaling factors

Generality is addressed via additional non-R1 model families (GPT-OSS distilled model), multiple model sizes, base-model comparisons, and extensive appendices covering annotation robustness, test-time compute, RAG validation, and case studies

Honest scoping: the paper explicitly acknowledges confounds (e.g., dynamic quantization calibration differences, inability to compare under identical calibration) and provides justifications for methodological choices
weaknesses: The interpretability analysis is largely restricted to small models (R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Qwen-7B); the claimed generalization of key findings rests on limited evidence outside these settings, and the 'greatly surpassing state-of-the-art' claim for the 6.57% gain is based on a single model (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) with a simple heuristic protection scheme, without testing on other architectures or bit-widths

Annotation of reasoning behaviors relies entirely on GPT-4o with only 120 instances; the human validation in Appendix G samples just 10 instances per behavior, and the confidence interval for 'adding knowledge' includes negative correlation, leaving annotation reliability partially unverified

Several conclusions conflate model size (parameter count) with the compression method itself, e.g., the claim that pruning/distillation hurt knowledge more than reasoning is largely inferred from MuSiQue scores that also vary with model family (Qwen vs. Llama base models differ in pretraining data)

The theoretical grounding of the adapted attribution patching / difference-of-means pipeline is thin; the equivalence between steering-vector-gradient inner products and causal weight importance is assumed rather than analyzed, and counterfactual/patching validation beyond selective quantization of a handful of components is limited

Inconsistent rigor in validation: Table 3 shows an exception (1_up lowest on AIME 2024) that contradicts the importance ranking, explained post hoc in Appendix N; the protection experiment lacks comparison against a natural baseline of protecting an equal number of unimportant weights
No release of code/annotation data is mentioned, and reproduction of the full pipeline (GPT-4o annotation, heatmaps, mixed-precision protection) would be difficult from the description alone

strengths: Comprehensive empirical scope: the paper benchmarks quantization (dynamic/2.51–1.58 bit, AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3), distillation (four R1-distilled models), and pruning (SparseGPT, AlphaPruning) on reasoning-specific datasets, filling a genuine gap since most compression studies evaluate only perplexity or simple end tasks.

Novel application of mechanistic interpretability (difference-of-means steering vectors + attribution patching) at the level of every linear module, going beyond the layer-wise analysis of prior work, and addressing the practically important question of locating critical weights for reasoning.

Findings are supported by verification experiments rather than only correlational heatmaps: selective 3-bit quantization of the final-layer up projection (0.7% of weights, 16.3% average drop), selective protection of final-layer MLP modules (+6.57% average over 3-bit AWQ, up to 23.17%), AWQ scaling-factor diagnosis, and a RAG experiment to decouple knowledge memorization from reasoning.

Useful practical takeaways (weight count matters more for knowledge than reasoning; collapse point correlates with benchmark difficulty; current quantizers over-compress final-layer modules and MLP gate projections), plus evidence of generalization to a non-R1 distilled model and useful appendices (test-time compute, collapse case studies).
weaknesses: Statistical fragility of the core benchmarking claims: AIME 2024 has only 30 problems and MuSiQue 100 sampled questions, so many reported differences (e.g., 2.51-bit R1 'beating' R1, 3–6 point gaps between quantizers) correspond to 1–2 problems; no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for Table 1, undermining fine-grained comparisons between methods.

The interpretation pipeline rests on a chain of approximations whose causal validity is under-justified: GPT-4o annotation of four reasoning behaviors, steering vectors averaged over short token windows, and attribution patching using cross-entropy loss gradients as a proxy for 'reasoning importance.' The human validation is very small (10 sampled instances per behavior) and the 'adding knowledge' correlation is essentially unvalidated (Spearman ρ=0.486, CI [−0.218, 1.000]), yet conclusions are drawn across all four behaviors uniformly.

Several headline findings are somewhat expected or incremental: that parameter count/pruning harms parametric knowledge more than reasoning, and that quantization degrades final-layer and gate projections, largely confirm known intuitions (e.g., AWQ's activation-aware salience already protects important channels); the mechanistic analysis mostly re-derives what activation statistics already suggest, as partially conceded in Appendix M.

The 'surpassing the state-of-the-art' claim (finding 3) is overstated: the proposed 'protection' is simply keeping ~2% of weights in 16-bit, evaluated only against 3-bit AWQ on one 8B model and one benchmark suite, without comparison to established mixed-precision or outlier-protection baselines or to other quantizers with the same protection applied.

Generalization claims are thin: 'findings generalize to non-R1 families' rests on a single 4B distilled model with one-pass scores, and the mechanistic analysis is largely confined to 7B/8B models where interpretability is feasible, while the strongest compression results concern the 671B MoE model that is never mechanistically analyzed.

The justification for visualizing only importance decreases (Section 2.3, Appendix H) embeds an assumption (compression only harms, never redistributes, importance) that biases the analysis toward confirming the paper's bottleneck narrative; the net-change analysis is relegated to an appendix and does not fully resolve the concern.

Mixed presentation quality and some internal inconsistencies (e.g., pruned-model comparisons limited to the 'usable' regime, exceptions like 1_up on AIME 2024 explained post hoc as 'random perturbation'), which weaken confidence in the rigor of conclusions drawn from noisy small-sample results.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and timely question—how compression (quantization, distillation, pruning) affects large reasoning models—with a comprehensive benchmark across multiple model sizes, compression methods, and four reasoning benchmarks of varying difficulty, providing a valuable reference for practitioners.

The mechanistic interpretation component is a genuine contribution: adapting difference-of-means steering vectors and attribution patching to compute module-level weight importance, going beyond prior layer-wise analyses and directly connecting interpretability to the practical problem of locating critical weights for compression.

The findings are empirically validated rather than merely observational: selective quantization of the final-layer up_proj (Table 3), cross-family generalization (Qwen, non-R1 DistilGPT-OSS model in Appendix J), alignment with AWQ scaling factors (Appendix M), and a mixed-precision protection mechanism that yields a 6.57% average accuracy gain, surpassing existing 3-bit baselines (Table 4).

Careful experimental hygiene: three-pass evaluation, collapse-point analysis across sparsity levels (Table 2), test-time compute analysis (Appendix O), RAG experiments to decouple knowledge from reasoning (Appendix L), and annotation robustness checks for the GPT-4o labeling pipeline (Appendix G).

Findings are presented with actionable takeaways (e.g., protect final-layer MLP modules and gate projections; prefer quantization over pruning/distillation for knowledge-intensive tasks) that could directly guide future compression method design.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: both difference-of-means and attribution patching are existing interpretability techniques adapted to a new setting; the paper is primarily an empirical study rather than a new method or technique.

The attribution patching importance scores are linear approximations, yet claims of 'causal relationships between weights and reasoning capabilities' are somewhat overstated; the single validation per finding (one matrix quantized, one protection experiment) is limited, and the protection experiment is only run on R1-Distill-Llama-8B with 3-bit AWQ, not across the other quantizers or model families it generalizes to.

Several benchmark sizes are very small (AIME 2024 has 30 questions; MuSiQue is subsampled to 100), so per-model differences of a few points carry high variance; some conclusions (e.g., 2.51-bit outperforming R1 itself on average) may be noise artifacts of small sample sizes.

The knowledge-vs-reasoning dichotomy (Key Finding 1) rests almost entirely on MuSiQue scores under a closed-book setting; a single benchmark is a narrow basis for the broad claim that 'weight count impacts knowledge memorization more than reasoning'.

Attribution of the 'overly compressed' modules to method failure is somewhat confounded: dynamic quantization cannot be compared under identical calibration, and differences between MoE (R1) and dense (distilled) architectures are acknowledged but not disentangled.

Some findings may partially reflect known effects of final-layer/outlier roles in transformers (e.g., Liu et al., 2025b on principal weights after reasoning SFT), and the paper could better position the incremental insight relative to these concurrent analyses.
